definitions.gloss: Kikunae Ikeda; the chemist who discovered umami
definitions.explanation: A chemist (1864–1936) at Tokyo Imperial University who in 1908 isolated glutamate from {昆布|こんぶ} and named the taste うま{味|み}. His work led directly to the commercial seasoning {味|あじ}の{素|もと}.

examples.japanese: うま{味|み}を{発見|はっけん}したのは{池田菊苗|いけだきくなえ}だ。
examples.english: It was Kikunae Ikeda who discovered umami.

examples.japanese: {池田菊苗|いけだきくなえ}は{昆布|こんぶ}のだしからグルタミン{酸|さん}を{取|と}り{出|だ}した。
examples.english: Ikeda extracted glutamate from kelp stock.

examples.japanese: {池田菊苗|いけだきくなえ}が1908{年|ねん}に{名付|なづ}けた「うま{味|み}」は、{今|いま}では umami として{世界中|せかいじゅう}で{通用|つうよう}する。
examples.english: The word umami, coined by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908, is now understood worldwide.

notes:
The name is read {池田|いけだ} (family name) + {菊苗|きくなえ} (given name); {菊苗|きくなえ} is unusual enough that the reading is often given in furigana even in Japanese texts.

COMMON EXPRESSIONS:
- {池田菊苗|いけだきくなえ}のうま{味|み}{発見|はっけん}: Ikeda's discovery of umami
- {日本|にほん}の{十大|じゅうだい}{発明|はつめい}: "Japan's ten great inventions," a list his seasoning patent is always on

CULTURAL NOTE:
He is a fixture of school science lessons and of any discussion of Japanese food abroad, because umami is the one taste term Japanese has given the world's languages. He also studied in Leipzig under Wilhelm Ostwald and roomed in London with the novelist {夏目漱石|なつめそうせき}.
